item.description:
⟡ Where the Light Goes in January
A direct flight from Gatwick to Mauritius in January takes eleven hours and fifty-five minutes. A direct flight to Madeira from the same airport takes under four. One buys you thirteen hours of daylight a day, the other barely changes what the sky was already doing at home.
We compared six winter-sun coasts this week: flight time, daylight hours, and the weather each one is likely to bring, region by region, no sales pitch attached. Come in and we'll talk you through which trade suits you.

item.title: ⟡ The Caribbean's honest season
item.description:
⟡ The Caribbean's honest season
The Atlantic hurricane season runs from the first of June to the thirtieth of November, officially, so January sits nowhere near it, whatever you might have assumed. Barbados and St Lucia both fly nonstop from the UK, around nine hours either way, into a dry season that runs December through May.
It's the shortest daylight of the three oceans we compared this week, over eleven hours, but it's about as dependable as winter sun gets if a settled week matters more to you than the miles. Come in and we'll show you where.

item.title: ⟡ The number we won't give you
item.description:

We looked for a January sea-temperature reading from a national meteorological service, from NOAA, or from Europe's own ocean-monitoring service, for six winter-sun coasts. None of them publish one. Every figure in circulation traces back to a booking site with no source behind it, so we're not handing you one we can't stand behind.
What we can tell you: Madeira gets you out of a British January in around four hours, and it still finds room for real rain. The Red Sea trades an extra ninety minutes in the air for genuinely warm, dry days. Different trip, different truth. Come and tell us which one sounds like yours.

item.title: Northern Spain eclipse (Tue 11 Aug) [NEEDS IMAGE]
item.description:
Some journeys can wait; this one has a date on it, and you can't move it. 🖤
On 12 August a total solar eclipse crosses northern Spain. From Oviedo, totality runs one minute and forty-eight seconds, starting at 20:27, with the sun only a few degrees above the horizon.
That's the point of it. The shadow comes at you across the ground before it reaches the sky, the light goes the colour of old brass, and you stand in it with the sea at your back.
The path comes ashore in Galicia and runs east through Asturias and León towards Zaragoza and the Balearics. Check the centre line before you book, because the edges give you a partial and nothing more.
At Agent Nouveau, we gather the trips that have to happen on the day. 🖤

item.title: Kotor, Montenegro (Wed 12 Aug) [NEEDS IMAGE]
item.description:
Some towns are about arriving; this one is about the moment you look up. 🖤
Kotor is folded into the far end of its bay in Montenegro, where the mountains come down so steeply that the walled town has nowhere to go but inward.
The old town has been UNESCO listed since 1979, and the walls wrapping it run four and a half kilometres. From inside them, 1,350 steps climb the rock to the fortress of San Giovanni, 280 metres up. Go at first light, before the heat, and take more water than you think you need.
Come back down for grilled fish by the water, and you'll understand why people keep this place to themselves.

Destination Spotlight: A Tuscan borgo reopened as a hotel, and the quiet you go there for. ✦
Chapter Chianti opened in June inside a restored medieval borgo, the old stone village rebuilt room by room rather than replaced. There are eighty-two rooms across ninety-nine acres, Tristan du Plessis did the interiors, and the furniture was made by hand nearby.
You notice the quiet before you notice the room. At six in the evening the only thing moving is the light going off the stone.
It's forty-five minutes from Florence and the same from Siena, so you can take either as a day out and still be back for dinner at Osso. Bring a car and no fixed plan for lunch. That's how the week finds you.

item.title: Madeira (Sun 16 Aug) [NEEDS IMAGE]
item.description:
We're dreaming of Madeira this morning, where you walk level and the water walks beside you. ✦
The levadas are irrigation channels cut from the fifteenth century onwards by men called rocheiros, roped over cliff faces to carry water from the wet north-west to the dry south-east. More than three thousand kilometres survive, and the paths running alongside them go everywhere the water goes, which on this island is everywhere.
You'll walk through laurisilva, the relict laurel forest that once covered southern Europe and now holds on here, UNESCO listed, with the drop on one side and the channel running past your boot.
Funchal takes care of the evenings. The island barely has a winter, so it works in the months when nothing at home does.

item.title: Sardinia (Tue 18 Aug) [NEEDS IMAGE]
item.description:
Some islands are about the coast; this one asks you to turn inland. 🖤
Archaeologists working at Carrarzu Iddia, near Bortigali, uncovered a Giants' Tomb this summer, hidden under scrub at 740 metres. It came to light during survey and restoration work on the site.
You come up to it through that scrub, and it's quiet in a way the coast never is. The stone is trachyte, dark and volcanic. The forecourt still curves the way it was built to, so you stand where people stood to bury their dead.
Tombs like it start appearing around 1800 BC, alongside the nuraghi, the conical towers you find here by the thousand and nowhere else. Give the interior a day, start at Su Nuraxi in Barumini, and you'll come home with a different island in your head.
At Agent Nouveau, we find the islands with something underneath them. 🖤

item.title: Danieli, Venezia (Sun 23 Aug) [NEEDS IMAGE]
item.description:
Destination Spotlight: The quiet return of a Venetian landmark. ✦
On 26 August the Danieli reopens as Danieli, Venezia, A Four Seasons Hotel, after more than three years closed.
It's always been three palaces rather than one, and the oldest, Palazzo Dandolo, went up in 1471. Pierre-Yves Rochon has pulled the palette off the lagoon itself, celadon and powder pink and terracotta, so the morning light coming up off the water finds a room already the same colour as it. The Murano glass does the rest. It opens with 120 rooms and suites.
If you've walked the Riva degli Schiavoni and wondered what sat behind those hoardings, here's your answer. Ask us for a room facing the water, and tell us how you want to wake up.

item.title: Amura, Mount Nelson (Mon 10 Aug)
item.description:
Destination Spotlight: Six Michelin stars, four nights, and one kitchen you want a seat in. ✦
Amura is Ángel León's restaurant at Mount Nelson, A Belmond Hotel, the pink hotel that's stood above Cape Town's Government Avenue since 1899. From 13 to 16 August, Alain Roux is cooking there too.
León holds three stars at Aponiente in Cádiz, where he built a restaurant around the sea itself. Roux is chef-patron at The Waterside Inn on the Thames, which has held three since 1985. He's bringing the raspberry soufflé that's been on that menu for fifty years. He cooks the first three nights; on the sixteenth, León joins him at the pass.
August is winter down there, and it's the season Cape Town keeps for itself. The light is clear, the mountain is green, and you won't queue for any of it.

item.title: Granville, Normandy (Fri 14 Aug)
item.description:
We're dreaming of Granville this morning, and a pink house above the Normandy sea you can still walk through. ✦
Villa Les Rhumbs is where Christian Dior grew up. It takes its name from the thirty-two points of a compass rose, which tells you something about a house that faces the Channel head on. It's now the Musée Christian Dior.
His mother Madeleine made the garden, and you can still walk it, wind coming off the Channel and the roses holding on in it. The museum's argument is that the couture came out of this patch of ground, and standing in it, you believe them.
The current show runs to 1 November. Granville's a working port, so there are oysters, and a boat out to the Îles Chausey if you want the sea to yourself.

item.title: Luura – Cliff, Paros (Sat 15 Aug)
item.description:
Destination Spotlight: Thirty-nine suites cut into a Parian cliff, and the calm of the middle Cyclades. ✦
Luura has opened above the bay of Agia Irini on the west coast of Paros. It's adults only, all suites, and nineteen of them have a pool of their own. Elastic Architects did the buildings and Lambs and Lions the interiors, and it's Cycladic without any of the fancy dress.
The wind drops around seven here. The water goes flat, the bay turns the colour of the inside of a shell, and you're still deciding between Mimi Kakushi for the Japanese and Lenea for the Mediterranean.
Paros spent years in the shadow of its louder neighbours. If you want that light without the ferry queue, come to the middle of the archipelago.

item.title: Beaverbrook, Surrey (Mon 17 Aug)
item.description:
Destination Spotlight: An hour from London, and a world of calm away from it. ✦
Beaverbrook sits in the Surrey Hills at Cherkley Court, a house built in the 1860s and bought in 1911 by Lord Beaverbrook, who lived there fifty years and had Churchill and Kipling to stay.
The Dower House, five bedrooms of it, has been reworked by Nicola Harding. The Garden House looks straight over the kitchen gardens, so lunch arrives smelling faintly of whatever was cut that morning, and there's a Japanese grill in the main house for the evening.
Leave after breakfast and you're walking the grounds by mid-morning, with a whole afternoon to lose in them and nobody to meet. That's the point of it, and you feel it again on the drive home.

item.title: Castle of Mey (Thu 20 Aug)
item.description:
We're dreaming of the far north of Scotland this morning, and the last castle before you run out of mainland. ✦
The Castle of Mey was built in 1566 and stands on the Caithness coast looking over the Pentland Firth to Orkney. It'd been left near-derelict when the Queen Mother saw it in 1952, bought it, and gave it back its old name.
She had it restored inside three years, then came every August and October for the next fifty, the last of them in the autumn of 2001. The walled garden needs a twelve-foot wall, the Great Wall of Mey, to keep the salt wind off it.
You get long light up here in August, and gannets.

item.title: The Francis Hotel, Bath (Fri 21 Aug)
item.description:
Destination Spotlight: The Francis has come back to Queen Square, and Bath is calmer than you think. ✦
Fourteen million pounds went into it, across all ninety-eight rooms, on a square that earned the money. Queen Square was the first of Bath's Georgian set pieces, designed by John Wood the Elder, who lived in the terrace himself. It became a hotel in 1884, when Emily Francis ran seven adjoining houses together into one.
Emberwood, the new brasserie, opened in May, and a thermal spa follows this year, so you don't have to walk out to find dinner.
Bath rewards you for staying overnight. The day trippers leave around five, the crescents empty, and the honey-coloured stone is yours in the evening light.

item.title: Sumba / NIHI (Sat 22 Aug)
item.description:
We're dreaming of Sumba this morning, and of a horse that reads you better than most people do. ✦
Sumba sits east of Bali and feels a century away from it: dry grassland, carved stone tombs standing in the villages, and the Marapu faith still running under daily life.
NIHI keeps a herd of twenty-two Sandalwood ponies, the island's own small breed, named for the trees that once covered the place. In the equine sessions you stand with one rather than ride it, and it responds to how you're standing there. Most people find that harder than riding.
Afterwards you can take one down to the sand and into the surf, which is the other thing this coast is known for.

item.title: White Elephant Aspen
item.description:
Destination Spotlight: Nantucket's harbourfront grande dame has learned to ski. ✦
White Elephant opened its first mountain address on 15 June, at the corner of Main and Garmisch in Aspen's West End. The 54 rooms trade the brand's seaside whites for charcoal and saddle leather, embossed headboards and hand-painted lampshades, with vintage skis and small brass elephants hiding in the details.
More than 125 original artworks hang through the house, Alex Katz landscapes among them, and LoLa 41 makes the trip west too… sushi and a raw bar by night, the year-round heated pool steaming through the seasons outside.
A Nantucket institution, now with an alpine address to match.

item.title: The Peloponnese, on foot
item.description:
Some walks are about the summit; this one is about everything between. 🕶️
Greece is joining some 1,700 kilometres of old paths into the Peloponnese Trails, its largest walking network… twelve linked routes across the peninsula Homer filled with kings and homecomings, passing Mycenae, Epidaurus and Olympia on the way.
A week of it runs along centuries-old mule tracks re-marked through olive groves, past stone villages like Dimitsana and Stemnitsa appearing out of Arcadian forest, down to a swim where the mountains meet the sea, and always to a table under a plane tree at the end of the stage.
The Odyssey took ten years. A fortnight here feels like a fair abridgement.
At Agent Nouveau, we walk the routes worth taking at walking pace. 🖤

item.title: St Benedict, St Leonards-on-Sea
item.description:
Destination Spotlight: a seaside house where the nineteenth century never checked out. ✦
St Benedict stands in St Leonards-on-Sea, an 1881 house that owners Paul Oxborrow and Stephen Groves have spent decades returning to itself… the staircase moved back to its original position, the servants' bells rehung, the larder shelved in slate.
The six rooms each keep a story. The Colonel's Room holds a half-tester bed and a roll-top bath; The School Room is papered in nineteenth-century alphabet print; Watts of Westminster hangs in the hall. Breakfast arrives as silver service, as the house would expect.
An hour and a half from London, and a century further than that.

item.title: Grosvenor Square, London
item.description:
We're dreaming of London this morning… of a square that waited three hundred years to become a garden again. 🖤
Grosvenor Square reopened on 20 July after a £25 million remaking by Tonkin Liu: 150,000 new plants and bulbs, 44 young trees, wetlands folded into Mayfair, and the oval lawn from the 1720s reinstated at the centre of it all.
Late summer there means crossing from Mount Street with the borders in first flower, finding one of the 300 new seats, and watching Mayfair remember it was built around a green.
Some openings this year are hotels. The loveliest one in London might be a lawn.

item.title: Locanda Cipriani, Torcello
item.description:
Destination Spotlight: the lagoon inn where Hemingway kept a room has reopened its doors. ✦
We've been waiting for this one. Locanda Cipriani came back to Torcello in June, after a two-year restoration that grew the 1936 inn from six rooms to ten… four new suites, half opening straight onto the replanted rose gardens, the others finished in marble beside the canal.
Fabrizio Cocchi's brief was preservation, not reinvention. The ceiling beams are repainted white, the new light fittings blown by Vetreria Venier on Murano, and the dining room still serves the Cipriani classics that kept Hemingway here long enough to write a novel, with the bell tower of Santa Maria Assunta standing watch over the vine pergola.
Ninety years on, still the slowest address in the lagoon. Long may it stay that way.

item.title: The Riviera di Ulisse, Lazio
item.description:
We're dreaming of the Riviera di Ulisse this morning… the coastline that kept its myths close. 🖤
Halfway between Rome and Naples it runs… the stretch of Lazio shore where Homer's hero is said to have wandered, and where the emperor Tiberius built a dining room inside a sea cave at Sperlonga, its marble Odyssey scenes found again in 1957.
Imagine whitewashed lanes stacked above the water, a morning swim below Monte Circeo, the headland the ancients named as Circe's island… then an evening climb to Terracina's Temple of Jupiter Anxur, suspended between land and sea.
The Amalfi crowds are two hours south. The mythology is right here.

item.title: San Sebastián
item.description:
We're dreaming of San Sebastián this evening… of the hour when the Parte Vieja starts to fill and the counters disappear under pintxos. 🕶️
The local rhythm goes like this: one or two bites and a glass of txakoli at each bar, ordered from the blackboard, then on to the next stop, the way the txikiteros have always done it. When the appetite needs a pause, the 1912 wooden funicular climbs Monte Igueldo, and the whole curve of La Concha opens below.
Nineteen Michelin stars sit within 25 kilometres of this small Basque city. The best plate of the night may still be the one balanced on the bar.

Destination Spotlight: the Belle Époque palace across the bay from Saint-Tropez is taking guests again. ✦
COMO Le Beauvallon opened its doors in April, the first full season for the 1914 hotel after nearly two decades reserved for private events. Churchill, Colette and Fitzgerald knew it in its first life; the guest book is ready for new names.
The estate runs ten acres from Provençal hillside down to the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, with Yannick Alléno cooking at Beauvallon Sur Mer on the water, a Toyo Ito Serpentine pavilion standing on the lawns, and a boat that crosses to Saint-Tropez port in eight minutes.
The town keeps the noise. The palace keeps the bay.

item.title: Charleston Harbor
item.description:
Some harbours are for photographing; Charleston's is for settling into. 🕶️
The city's waterfront gained a new anchor this spring: The Cooper, 191 rooms above Charleston Harbor with interiors by Champalimaud, a grand lawn running straight into Joe Riley Waterfront Park, and its own marina with a Hinckley yacht ready for charters.
Imagine the day built around the water… oysters and a seafood tower at The Crossing, an afternoon at the waterfront infinity pool with the harbour going gold, cocktails at Bar Marti four floors above the tide. Then the old city behind you: pastel terraces, palmettos, church bells.
A city famous for its manners now keeps a front porch on the water.

item.title: The Chairman's Train
item.description:
Destination Spotlight: Britain's only privately owned heritage train is taking bookings. ✦
The Chairman's Train launched in May from Locomotive Services' Crewe works: nine former Caledonian Sleeper carriages rebuilt for private hire, dressed by designer Sara Oliver in walnut panelling, George Smith velvet and a 1950s-style livery, with a baby grand piano in the lounge car.
The details understand rail life. Marble basins, Roberts radios, walk-in showers… and our favourite, magnetic strips under the champagne glasses, because the West Highland Line has curves. Charters take two to sixteen guests; this summer's five-day Scottish journeys leave from London Euston.
One train, sixteen berths, and the whole map of Britain to choose from.

item.title: Barcelona, the Gaudí centenary

item.description:

The postcard is the palace. The pulse is the street behind it.

item.title: Split and Pula, Croatia
item.description:
Some ruins you visit; in Croatia, you check in and live inside them. 🖤
We keep sending people to Split and Pula, two Adriatic towns where the Roman world never fully left. In Split, Diocletian built his retirement palace at the end of the third century, and the old town simply grew up inside its walls, cafés and courtyards tucked between eighteen-hundred-year-old stone.
Imagine an evening in Pula, where the amphitheatre still stands nearly whole, twenty thousand seats open to the sky, a concert filling it as crowds once filled it when Rome was young. Then a plate of Istrian truffle and a glass of Malvazija as the light goes soft. History here is not behind glass. It pours the wine.
Two coasts, one long memory. Come stay inside it.
At Agent Nouveau, we find the places where the past is still in use. ✦

item.title: Waldorf Astoria London, Admiralty Arch
item.description:
Destination Spotlight: The arch the whole of London walks under is about to let people stay the night. ✦
We're watching Waldorf Astoria London, Admiralty Arch, the Edwardian landmark on The Mall that, for more than a century, was only ever something you passed through.
Sir Aston Webb designed it, the same hand behind the Buckingham Palace façade, and King Edward VII raised it in memory of Queen Victoria. No guest has ever spent a night inside. That changes in autumn 2026... reservations opened in June for a first-ever hotel of 114 rooms and suites, naval names like the Nelson and the Victory, dining from Clare Smyth and Daniel Boulud, and a spa set into the old stonework opposite the Palace.
A door the whole city knows, opening inward for the first time. Some landmarks are worth the wait to sleep in.
At Agent Nouveau, we find the rooms history kept locked until now. 🖤

item.title: Comporta, Alentejo (Portugal)
item.description:
Some coastlines are about being seen; this one is about being left alone. 🖤
We're dreaming of Comporta this morning... the stretch of Alentejo an hour south of Lisbon where the rice fields, not the resorts, still set the tone.
Imagine a place the Lisbon set has guarded since the 1950s and never quite told anyone about: low white houses under umbrella pines, wild Atlantic beaches with no one on them, storks nesting over the Sado estuary, and the stilt cabins of Carrasqueira leaning out over the tide. There are no high-rises, no strip of signage, no scene to perform for. The dress code is bare feet. Even now, with Sublime's new villas drawing a wider crowd, Comporta keeps its trick of making everyone pretend not to notice each other.
The Algarve gets the postcards. Comporta gets the people who would rather you didn't know.
At Agent Nouveau, we gather the places that stay quiet on purpose. ✦

item.description:

In 1925 a professor at Stellenbosch named Abraham Perold crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut and planted four seeds in his garden. He very nearly lost them. The seedlings were rescued from a clearance by a young lecturer who happened to be passing, and from those vines came Pinotage, a grape that grows seriously almost nowhere on earth but here.
It has not always been easy to love, and that is part of the point. No one argues about a wine with no character. The Cape has a red that belongs to it completely, the way few countries can say of any grape, and the best of it now is very good indeed.
